items.item: maxPartitionBytes caps the bytes packed into a single partition when reading files

at.deep: Input splits and target task size, the sourced-only half

items.item: openCostInBytes is the estimated cost of opening a file, padded in so small files don't over-crowd one partition

at.deep: Input splits and target task size, the sourced-only half

items.item: spark.sql.shuffle.partitions configures the number of partitions used when shuffling for joins or aggregations

at.step: Reveal: one config sets the count directly

items.item: the partition-splitting function takes maxSplitBytes and openCostInBytes together as the two inputs to one packing decision

at.deep: Input splits and target task size, the sourced-only half

items.item: The 100-200 MB per-task target size named in the syllabus clause is a guideline the Performance Tuning docs state in prose, not a config value this topic independently measures a task actually hitting — this topic measures partition count behaviour directly (shuffle.partitions, repartition, coalesce), disclosing the target-size guideline as sourced-only.

at.out: the ~100-200 MB per-task target size named as a sourced guideline; not independently measured against a real task's own bytes

items.item: spark.sql.files.minPartitionNum and spark.sql.files.maxPartitionNum (both named in the same Performance Tuning docs table this topic quotes from) are two further input-split levers beyond maxPartitionBytes and openCostInBytes — named only, not independently measured, since this topic's own examples.py measures shuffle partitioning and repartition/coalesce, not file-read splitting specifically.

at.out: minPartitionNum/maxPartitionNum named only; not independently measured

items.item: repartition can also take column expressions (e.g. repartition(col)) to hash-partition by a key rather than an explicit count, producing an uneven-but-key-grouped result rather than the evenly-sized result this topic's own count-based measurement shows — a different call shape from the one this topic measures.

at.out: column-based repartition named only; this topic measures the count-based form

items.item: AQE's own coalescePartitions feature (spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled, on by default when AQE is on) automatically merges small shuffle partitions at runtime using a target size — a separate, automatic mechanism from the explicit .coalesce() call this topic measures, disabled throughout this topic's own examples.py (AQE off) specifically so the manual partition counts measured are Catalyst's own up-front numbers, not a runtime-adjusted count.

at.out: AQE's automatic coalescePartitions named only; disabled throughout this topic's own measurement

items.item: A coalesce call that reduces the partition count but not all the way to one still narrows upstream parallelism, proportionally — collapsing 8 partitions to 3 means roughly 3 tasks now cover the work 8 tasks did, a smaller version of the same mechanism this topic's own coalesce(1) measurement demonstrates at its most extreme.

at.step: Reveal: no shuffle, and no growing either

items.item: repartitionByRange (distinct from the hash-based column form) partitions by sorted range boundaries rather than a hash of the key, intended for range-based downstream scans rather than even load — named only, not independently measured, a third repartition shape alongside the count-based and hash-based ones.

at.out: repartitionByRange named only; a third repartition shape not independently measured

items.item: Calling coalesce immediately after a wide shuffle operation (rather than directly on a narrow read, as this topic's own examples.py does) still avoids adding a second shuffle, but the task count it collapses to is the shuffle's own existing output partition count, not an upstream read's partition count — the same narrow-merge mechanism, applied one stage later in the plan.

at.out: coalesce-after-shuffle named only; this topic's own measurement applies coalesce directly to a narrow read

items.item: This topic's own repartition/coalesce measurements use spark.range's own numPartitions argument to fix a clean, Exchange-free 8-partition starting point deliberately, specifically so any Exchange node found afterward can only have come from the repartition or coalesce call itself, not from upstream lineage.

at.out: the methodology choice of an Exchange-free base, disclosed to isolate each call's own plan contribution

items.item: spark.sql.files.minPartitionNum defaults to spark.sql.leafNodeDefaultParallelism when unset, meaning the actual minimum partition count for a small file-based read depends on cluster size even when maxPartitionBytes alone would suggest fewer, larger partitions.

at.out: spark.sql.files.minPartitionNum's own default resolution named only; not independently measured

items.item: CoalescedRDD (the RDD-level implementation coalesce compiles down to) groups parent partitions using a locality-aware algorithm by default, preferring to merge partitions that already sit on the same executor — a scheduling detail beyond the partition-count behaviour this topic's own examples.py measures directly.

at.out: CoalescedRDD's own locality-aware grouping named only; this topic measures resulting partition count and plan shape, not scheduling locality
